Feebleness
FEE-bul-nes
n. (weakness, especially of the hands; the collapse of a man's grip under terror)
From Old French feble, from Latin flebilis, lamentable, from flere, to weep. At Jeremiah 47:3 it renders Hebrew riphyon, a slackening or sinking, from raphah, to let drop.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah is describing the Philistine coast under the approach of an army, and the horror is located in one detail: At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his strong horses, at the rushing of his chariots, and at the rumbling of his wheels, the fathers shall not look back to their children for feebleness of hands. The prophet does not describe the killing. He describes fathers running and not turning round. The Hebrew word is a slackening, a letting-drop, and it is used of hands because the hands are where terror shows first — a man whose hands have gone will not carry a child.

The Bible uses this bodily fact as a standing figure for the loss of courage. Ezekiel: All hands shall be feeble, and all knees shall be weak as water. Nahum, over Nineveh: the heart melteth, and the knees smite together. And because it is a figure, it can be reversed by a word. Isaiah gives the command that the writer to the Hebrews later takes up almost verbatim: Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees, which Hebrews turns into lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees and sets in the middle of a passage on chastening. That is the New Testament's pastoral use of the word. Hands that hang down are not rebuked; they are lifted, and the argument used to lift them is that the Father who is disciplining them is dealing with them as with sons.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): weakness; imbecility; want of strength; infirmity of body.

expand to see more

FEEBLENESS, n. Weakness of body or of mind; imbecility; infirmity; want of strength.

FEEBLE, a. Weak; destitute of much physical strength; infirm; debilitated.

SLACKEN, v.i. To become less tense, firm or rigid; to lose strength or intensity.

CONFIRM, v.t. To make firm or more firm; to add strength to; to strengthen.

RUMBLING, ppr. Making a low, heavy, continued sound, as of thunder or of wheels.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 47:3 — "At the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his strong horses, at the rushing of his chariots, and at the rumbling of his wheels, the fathers shall not look back to their children for feebleness of hands;"

Ezekiel 7:17 — "All hands shall be feeble, and all knees shall be weak as water."

Isaiah 35:3 — "Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees."

Hebrews 12:12 — "Wherefore lift up the hands which hang down, and the feeble knees;"

Modern Corruption

Discouragement is treated either as a moral failure to be scolded or as a condition to be managed, where Scripture commands the strong to go and strengthen the hands that have dropped.

expand to see more

Two responses to a discouraged Christian both miss what Isaiah and Hebrews prescribe. The first tells him to pull himself together, which is precisely what feeble hands cannot do; the second files him permanently under the weak and stops expecting anything of him. The biblical command is in the imperative and is addressed to somebody else: Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees. Hebrews places that command in the middle of a chapter about the Father's discipline, which means the strengthening is done with truth — you are a son, this is a Father's hand, the end of it is the peaceable fruit of righteousness — and not with sentiment.

The second thing to hold is the picture's honesty. Jeremiah 47 is a father who does not look back at his own child because his hands have failed him. Scripture does not pretend that faith exempts a man from the body's reactions to terror. Isaiah 40 says the youths shall faint and be weary and the young men shall utterly fall, and then, in the same breath, that they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength. The strength is renewed; it is not native. That is why the cure in every one of these passages comes from outside the man — a word spoken to him, a hand lifting his.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew riphyon (H7510), a slackening; raphah (H7503), to let drop, to be slack; Greek paraluo (G3886), to weaken or paralyse.

expand to see more

Hebrew riphyon (H7510) — a slackness, a sinking; used once, of the hands of fleeing fathers.

Hebrew raphah (H7503) — to sink, to let drop; the same root as be still in Be still, and know that I am God.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to strengthen, to make firm; Isaiah's command over the weak hands.

Greek paraluo (G3886) — to loose alongside, to enfeeble; the participle in Hebrews 12:12.

Greek anorthoo (G461) — to set upright again; lift up the hands which hang down.

Usage

"“the fathers shall not look back to their children for feebleness of hands” — terror located in the grip."

"“Strengthen ye the weak hands” — a command addressed to somebody else."

"“lift up the hands which hang down” — set in a chapter about a Father's discipline."
